title: 2 Kings 14:15–22
context: The narrator closes the reign of Jehoash of Israel, repeating the notices of 13:12–13, and then follows Amaziah’s final years. A conspiracy drives him to Lachish, where he is killed, and he is buried in David’s city. The people of Judah make his sixteen-year-old son Azariah king, and Azariah rebuilds Elath. How the reign lengths in these chapters fit together is debated. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the instability of Judah’s throne and God’s preservation of David’s line.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash which he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jehoash’s acts, his might, and his war with Amaziah are referred to Israel’s chronicles. The formula closes his story.

Arminian readers see the narrator summing up a reign marked by real victories but continued idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes:
The wording closely repeats 13:12, so Jehoash’s closing notice appears twice in the narrative.

Reformed readers see the narrator framing the account of Amaziah’s defeat. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the structure of Kings.

verses.text: Jehoash slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel; and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash dies, is buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam his son reigns in his place. This also echoes 13:13.

Arminian readers see the transition to Jeroboam’s long reign, which follows in verses 23–29.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition rounds off the Israel–Judah conflict before the text returns to Amaziah’s final years.

Reformed readers see God continuing Jehu’s dynasty as promised (2 Kings 10:30). Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground.

verses.text: Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, fifteen years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah lives fifteen years after Jehoash’s death. The text measures his later life by the northern king.

Arminian readers see years in which Amaziah still had opportunity to walk faithfully before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse ties Judah’s chronology to Israel’s at this point, and how the figures combine is debated.

Reformed readers see God granting years under his providence. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep chronological conclusions tentative.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Amaziah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Amaziah’s acts are referred to the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. The summary is brief.

Arminian readers see the narrator moving quickly from Amaziah’s defeat to his end.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cited chronicle is not the canonical book of Chronicles; it appears to be a source no longer extant.

Reformed readers see Scripture selecting what serves its purpose. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about the selective nature of the history.

verses.text: They made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish; but they sent after him to Lachish and killed him there.
verses.arminianNotes:
A conspiracy forms against Amaziah in Jerusalem; he flees to Lachish, but they pursue him there and kill him. His reign ends violently, as his father’s did.

Arminian readers see the instability that followed his defeat.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not name the conspirators or state their motive, so interpreters should not supply one.

Reformed readers see human plots unfolding under God’s rule. Both traditions read this as shared ground and treat Amaziah’s end as narrative, without speculation.

verses.text: They brought him on horses, and he was buried at Jerusalem with his fathers in David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes:
They bring him back on horses, and he is buried with his fathers in David’s city. He receives a royal burial despite his end.

Arminian readers see dignity accorded to a king whose reign mixed right and failure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Burial in the city of David marks him as a legitimate king of Judah.

Reformed readers see continuity in David’s line despite turmoil. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the Davidic house endures even through assassinations and defeat.

verses.text: All the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the place of his father Amaziah.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people of Judah take sixteen-year-old Azariah and make him king in place of Amaziah. The people secure the succession.

Arminian readers see the community acting to preserve stable rule.
verses.reformedNotes:
Azariah is also known as Uzziah elsewhere (for example 2 Chronicles 26). His reign is narrated in 2 Kings 15.

Reformed readers see God preserving David’s line through a young king. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to the Davidic house.

verses.text: He built Elath and restored it to Judah. After that the king slept with his fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Azariah builds Elath and restores it to Judah, after the king sleeps with his fathers. Judah regains a southern outpost.

Arminian readers see Judah’s fortunes recovering after the defeat at Beth Shemesh under a new king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elath lay near the Gulf of Aqaba. ‘The king’ most likely refers to Amaziah, placing the work after his death, though the phrasing is compact.

Reformed readers see restoration under God’s hand. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
